articles.title: Microsoft Offers Voluntary Exit Scheme To Employees In India; Check Eligibility And Benefits
articles.description: Microsoft has opened a voluntary exit window for eligible employees across four countries, including India, as the technology company offers staff financial assistance and career transition support to leave the organisation. The programme will cover employees at internal job grade level 70 and below in participating teams in India, the US, the UK and Canada. In India, eligible employees are understood to have until December 1 to decide whether to accept the offer. Microsoft has around 23,000 employees in India, but the company has not specified how many of them qualify for the scheme. Globally, around 60,000 employees are eligible. Microsoft Exit Offer: What Employees Can Expect The package is understood to include one month's base salary for every completed year of service, along with health insurance and career transition services. The precise terms of the offer will be communicated directly to eligible employees through emails, according to the company. In a blog post, Amy Coleman, Microsoft's Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, described the Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) as a time-bound initiative for employees considering opportunities beyond the company. Coleman said the programme would give eligible staff another option to make a career move with support, while enabling participating business units to adjust their workforce as their requirements change. She also noted that the initiative was new for Microsoft and that the company would learn from its implementation. Scheme Will Not Cover All Microsoft Teams The voluntary exit programme will not be applied across Microsoft's entire workforce. Participation will depend on the priorities of individual businesses, customer commitments and workforce needs, Coleman said. The company has also indicated that employees will continue to have opportunities to build new skills and explore internal roles where suitable. “There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee,” Coleman said, highlighting the need to balance changing business requirements with employees' opportunities to develop and contribute within the organisation. Microsoft Commits $20.5 Billion To India Through 2029 Alongside the announcement, Microsoft reiterated its investment plans for India, with a focus on cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence and workforce development. A company spokesperson said Microsoft had committed $20.5 billion between 2025 and 2029 towards cloud and AI infrastructure, skilling and operations in the country. The spokesperson also said the company remained on track to fulfil its commitment to equip 20 million people in India with AI skills by 2030.

articles.title: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Regional stocks mostly rose
articles.description: Asia firms into Tokyo lunch: Japan and Korea stocks rise, AUD and NZD gain after Nasdaq lead Ethereum Foundation “dump” is a $6.4m treasury sale, not a crisis South Korea Q3 GDP grows 1.0%, beating forecasts as AI chip boom lifts exports China September industrial profits jump 14.4% y/y, rebounding from 4.2% in August Japan services PPI picks up to 3.7% as August revised lower, backing BoJ hike path PBOC sets USD/ CNY central rate at 6.7171 (vs. estimate at 6.6731) Japan September services PPI holds at 3.7% y/y, in line with forecast, before BoJ Greer warns $3.4 billion EU loan to Airbus may breach US-EU aircraft trade truce Alt headlines: Australia CPI preview: banks see 1.0% core rise, above the RBA’s 0.8% forecast RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac’s Ellis says read the data calls ROADMAP: Morgan Stanley sees three catalysts ending the correction to ~7150, then S&P 500 to 8,000 BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk ICYMI: Morgan Stanley sees 10%-15% more downside for Chinese offshore stocks before a bottom Goldman Sachs: AI buildout to add up to 50bp to US core PCE, but the boost is temporary NZIER Shadow Board majority backs 25bp RBNZ hike to 3% as oil and weaker kiwi bite Citadel Securities warns AI trade has little margin for error as three risks converge Carney says Canada has not budged as US trade deal looks less imminent than claimed investingLive Americas FX news wrap 26 Oct: Anthropic IPO puts AI back in focus as stocks rebound Solana trading bot Bloom drained of $947,000 in SOL as nine users’ wallets emptied Summary: Regional stocks mostly rose after a Nasdaq-led session on Wall Street, though China and Hong Kong lagged The KOSPI jumped 3.4% and the Korea Exchange triggered a sidecar after the sharp rise; the KOSDAQ gained 2.8% The Nikkei rose 1.7%, led by chip-related stocks The US dollar was slightly softer, AUD and NZD rallied, while USD/JPY moved higher as the yen weakened broadly Japan’s services PPI rose 3.7% y/y, up from a downwardly revised 3.5%; China’s industrial profits rebounded 14.4% y/y in September South Korea’s Q3 GDP grew 1.0% q/q, beating forecasts on AI chip-driven exports Oil edged lower despite continuing Saudi-Houthi exchanges, and gold traded sideways just above $4,000 Equities Asian equities were mostly firmer on Tuesday, picking up the positive lead from Wall Street, where a Nasdaq-led session improved sentiment. Mainland China and Hong Kong were the exceptions. South Korea led the gains. The KOSPI climbed 3.4%, and its sharp rise prompted the Korea Exchange to trigger a sidecar, a temporary halt on program trading used to cool rapid moves. The KOSDAQ added 2.8%. Third-quarter GDP data showed the economy grew 1.0% from the previous quarter, well above the 0.7% forecast, as the global AI chip boom lifted exports and investment. The Bank of Korea estimates chips are driving about half of growth, although private consumption fell for the first time in nearly four years. In Japan, the Nikkei 225 rose 1.7%, with chip-related stocks leading the advance. In China, the Shanghai Composite slipped 0.1%, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 0.4%. Data Japan’s services producer price index rose 3.7% year on year in September, in line with forecasts and up from a downwardly revised 3.5% in August. The index is watched by the Bank of Japan for signs that firms are passing rising labour costs on to prices. The BoJ concludes its policy meeting on Friday and is expected to hold rates at 1.25% while signalling readiness for further hikes. China’s industrial profits rose 14.4% year on year in September, rebounding from 4.2% growth in August. Year-to-date growth eased slightly to 15.5% from 15.7%. Currencies The US dollar was slightly softer across much of the board. The Australian and New Zealand dollars both rallied, with Australia’s quarterly CPI data due on Wednesday. USD/JPY moved higher, bucking the broader dollar softness, as the yen weakened across the board. Commodities Oil prices edged slightly lower despite continuing exchanges between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, a reminder that Middle East supply risk remains in the background. Gold traded mostly sideways, holding just above $4,000 an ounce. Canada Hopes for a quick US-Canada trade agreement faded on Monday after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa has not changed its position in talks with Washington, and that any progress made so far reflects the US moving closer to Canada’s stance. The comments came as Semafor, citing sources, reported that a deal is likely not as imminent as US officials had suggested over the weekend. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: FCA Says Only 12% of CFD Firms Changed Charges: How Does Overnight Financing Fees Work?
articles.sourceName: Financial And Business News | Finance Magnates
articles.description: Most of the CFD firms the regulator surveyed looked again at their charges after its review, then kept them. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) surveyed 81 CFD firms in May 2026, six months after its November 2025 multi-firm review, and found that "only 12% of firms said they had changed any charges." Most of the rest explained their existing rates instead. The findings, published on 15 October and reported by Finance Magnates the next day, put one fee first among the FCA's remaining concerns: what a client pays to keep a position open overnight. What Finance Magnates found more telling than the 12% is that it sits at the bottom of the FCA's list of changes, where some firms changed, or planned to change, their calculation "to recognise that overnight financing is currently charged on total notional, with no interest paid on the initial margin posted by clients." That sentence captures much of the economics of the fee. Here is what the charge comprises, where it gets bigger than it looks, and how to compare it between brokers. What the Overnight Charge Is Built From What does a broker charge for holding a CFD overnight? Two pieces: a benchmark rate for the currency of the underlying and the broker's mark-up on top. IG's UK charges page puts its CFD admin fee at 1% for FX and 3% for other asset classes, charged on positions held past 10pm UK time. Its help page gives the index formula: Number of contracts × value per contract × price × (admin fee ± SONIA) ÷ 365. A 360-day divisor applies outside sterling, Singapore dollar and rand markets. Three days' funding is charged on positions held through Friday night. CMC Markets' holding costs page uses the same basic formula, with SONIA as the sterling benchmark. When the short side pays too A long pays the benchmark plus the mark-up. A short receives the benchmark minus it, which turns into a charge when the mark-up is bigger than the benchmark. CMC explains this for share CFDs. Sell positions are credited unless the interbank rate is at or below its add-on, in which case they "may incur a holding cost charge." It prices FX holding rates using the pair's tom-next rate. For commodities, both CMC and IG build the charge from the gap between futures prices, with their own fee on top. Where the Cost Gets Bigger Than It Looks Why is the charge on the full position, and what does that do? Because a CFD gives exposure to the full value of the underlying, the financing runs on the full value too. The FCA's November review said disclosures could be clearer about exactly that, including "charges being applied on the full consideration the CFD gives the client exposure to with no offset against the funds held on the client's account." It also highlighted the effect of leverage on the size of the charge relative to the client's own funds. The review found that most firms had considered paying interest on CFD account balances and decided not to. All figures below are illustrative assumptions, not any firm's terms. Daily charge = notional × (benchmark + mark-up) ÷ 365. Take a £50,000 long index position backed by £2,500 of margin, and a benchmark of 3.75%, using the Bank of England's Bank Rate as of October 2026. A client comparing 0.0171% and 0.0199% a day may never register a full percentage point of annual difference. The FCA says an annual rate "would give clients a more widely used comparison point." The last row shows the leverage effect the November review said disclosures could make clearer. The fee is small against the position value but large against the money the client actually put up. What happens when a client is long and short at once? Finance Magnates went looking for how a big UK name treats a hedged pair, and CMC puts it in one sentence: "holding costs are still charged on both sides regardless of your netting status." The FCA found the same at most of the firms it surveyed. Most firms charge matched positions, many call it an administration charge, and most apply "the same full funding charge spread" as on a genuine long or short. Run Broker B on a £50,000 long and a £50,000 short in the same index. The long pays 7.25% and the short receives 0.25%, leaving a net cost of £3,500 a year, or about £863 over 90 nights, for a position with no net market exposure. With the same spread on both legs, the net cost of a hedge is twice the mark-up, whatever the benchmark does. The FCA's sharper concern is firms that encourage matched positions with reduced or waived margin. It wants clients shown the pros and cons of this approach against simply closing the trade. What the FCA Found, and What It Wants What the 12% actually changed Four types of changes appear in the FCA's list of actions taken or planned by the 12% of firms that reported changing charges: Paying interest on cash balances. Cutting financing charges on matched or hedged positions. charges on outlier product groups after peer comparisons. Changing the calculation to recognise that clients earn nothing on their margin. The list includes planned changes as well as completed ones, so the 12% describes intent as well as action. On the changes firms did make, the FCA is blunt: they were "often designed to show that they have complied with the Duty, rather than materially changing their offering." The disclosure the regulator is asking for The FCA's good-practice list includes dedicated fee pages, pop-ups and deal-ticket information explaining how charges are calculated. These should provide information beyond the terms and conditions and key information documents (KIDs). Only a minority of firms have added an annual rate, and the FCA asks firms to consider whether outlier rates are compatible with fair value. There is no deadline and no new rule. The FCA says it will follow up with individual firms where it has concerns. The same week, it flagged surveillance gaps at seven retail brokers and said it would review appropriateness tests. Why Should Brokers Care? The transferable model is simple: at its core, the overnight charge is a benchmark plus a mark-up, applied to notional. The comparison question for any broker or asset class is then how big the mark-up is, what it is charged on, and whether the client can see it. Finance Magnates' read is that the annual percentage rate (APR) line is the cheapest fix on the FCA's list and probably the one that helps a client comparing two brokers most. Furthermore, Finance Magnates' gold swap survey shows what that looks like in one market. All 32 gold long readings it checked carried a negative swap, and the one credit on offer was a capped promotion. The FCA's findings have implications for several teams within a CFD broker. Two things may be worth watching into 2027: whether the FCA's individual follow-ups produce named outcomes, and whether interest on CFD cash balances spreads beyond the firms already planning it. Summary: What This Means Now The FCA has now said twice, eleven months apart, that some overnight charges may not represent fair value, and most firms answered with explanations rather than lower rates. The fee is a benchmark plus a mark-up on the full position, which makes it large against the margin a client posts and can double the mark-up on a hedge. The next round is individual follow-ups, and a firm that can show its rates as APRs against UK peers has its evidence ready. This article was written by Tareq Sikder at www.financemagnates.com.
